rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet is to call people to the true religion shared by all prophets, ignore enemy opposition, and hold firmly to what he was told.
rows.anchor: call people to this very religion of truth which is the common religion of all the prophets of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The phrase about not following their desires refers to fabricated religious innovations, which arise from desires.
rows.anchor: This is because these innovations spring from desires.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet's profession of faith in God's revealed Book answers opponents who want him to follow their religious innovations and desires.
rows.anchor: he has professed faith in the Book of God; so how can he follow their innovations and desires?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Prophet was sent to judge fairly among disputing groups, distinguish right from wrong, and disclose the true, unadulterated religion rather than follow their innovations.
rows.anchor: he has come to judge between them with justice; they have created disputes and differences in the religion of God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The warning reminds both believers and disbelievers that God is Lord of both groups and that both will ultimately stand before Him.
rows.anchor: it is God Who is the Lord of the believers and it is He Who is the Lord of the disbelievers

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Each side bears its own deeds: believers fulfill their duty by conveying the truth and are not answerable to God for the disbelievers' response.
rows.anchor: if the believers have communicated the truth to the disbelievers, then they have fulfilled their responsibility

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Once discussion and explanation have failed, there is no need to prolong debate; God will gather everyone, judge between them, and receive their return.
rows.anchor: there is no need to extend the conversation; the matter now rests with God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Muḥājjah means disputing and engaging in silly argument.
rows.anchor: means to dispute and to engage in silly arguments

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: In the phrase about disputing God, the omitted muḍāf is understood as referring to His oneness, since the dispute concerns tawḥīd.
rows.anchor: the muḍāf is suppressed ie.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Belief in God while associating partners with Him is religiously unacceptable; one must affirm Him as the one and only God, and disputing His oneness effectively negates Him.
rows.anchor: if someone disputes in the matter of His oneness, then it is as if He is disputing about God and actually negating Him.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The expression about dispute arising after acknowledgment means it arose after people had believed in God.
rows.anchor: this dispute has arisen after believing in God.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: All prophets from Noah to Jesus taught God's oneness, which the ancestors of the Quraysh, Jews, and Christians had acknowledged before their followers raised disputes.
rows.anchor: the teaching of all prophets from Noah (sws) to Jesus (sws) has been the same

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Given that prior acknowledgment, the later disputation is mere sophistry and will have no weight before God; it is destined to fail.
rows.anchor: Such silly argumentation is not going to avail them before God and is destined to be routed.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “The Book” refers to the Qur’an, and “the Balance” is an elucidation of the Book.
rows.anchor: to distinguish good from evil, the Qur’ ān was revealed by the Almighty as a scale of justice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Qur’an was revealed as a just standard for resolving disputes among the followers of earlier prophets and weighing truth against falsehood.
rows.anchor: the Qur’ ān was revealed by the Almighty as a scale of justice

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This verse restates the Prophet's declaration in 42:15 from another angle; 57:25 likewise pairs the Book and the Balance so people uphold justice, and the Qur’an is called muhaymin, a scale and barometer.
rows.anchor: Earlier, in verse 15, it had been declared from the tongue of the Prophet (sws)

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The eloquent warning says the Hour may be near: those who evade the Qur’an's just standard cannot escape the Day of Judgement's decision, so it is fortunate to settle disputes by that standard now.
rows.anchor: fortunate are the people who will distinguish between good and evil and resolve their differences

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Disbelievers treat the Hour as a bluff and insolently ask why it has not come, while believers recognize its horror and dread it.
rows.anchor: they are showing indifference to it; in fact, they obdurately remark: If it is to come, why is it not coming?

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The verse laments the deprivation of those disputing the obvious Hour: they have strayed far, and will awaken only when each faces an inescapable fate.
rows.anchor: expresses sorrow at the state of deprivation of these people who are disputing such an obvious reality as the Day of Judgement.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: God's mercy explains why He gives defiant people time: He provides for them without haste to punish, leaving them an opportunity to reform and become worthy of eternal mercy.
rows.anchor: God is very merciful to His servants, and takes the initiative in being merciful

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The other reason God gives the defiant time is that He is powerful and mighty.
rows.anchor: God is very powerful and mighty

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: This sūrah pairs with the previous one and shares its tawḥīd theme; the Hour underscores monotheism, while the discourse refutes angel divinity and intercession and the Quraysh claim that their polytheism came from Abraham.
rows.anchor: it is to highlight the importance of tawḥīd that the Day of Judgement is also mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After the previous sūrah highlighted the Qur’an's exaltedness from one angle, this one adds others and warns Quraysh, conceited over worldly wealth, that the Prophet's duty is to convey it while they bear responsibility for denial.
rows.anchor: the only responsibility of the Prophet (sws) was to communicate it to them; the responsibility of its denial will rest on them.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The sūrah shows that the Qur’an's call to tawḥīd matches the message of all earlier prophets; those rejecting it summon the doom that befell earlier rejecting nations.
rows.anchor: the harmony of the Qur’ ān with the message of the previous prophets is explained

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 1–8 describe God's favor to the Arabs through the Qur’an and the conclusive communication of truth, warning Quraysh that rejection will bring the fate of earlier nations, who were mightier.
rows.anchor: the conclusive communication of the truth as a result of it are mentioned

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Verses 9–15 note the opponents' confession that the Powerful and Knowledgeable God created the heavens and earth, despite their assigning partners among His servants; the universe's signs support tawḥīd and the Day of Judgement.
rows.anchor: The confession of the opponents of Islam that the Powerful and Knowledgeable God has created these heavens and the earth is referred to.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The reference to “my father and your father” points to God as Lord and sole object of worship, in the same sense that both speakers regard Him as father.
rows.anchor: in the same connotation they would regard Him to be the father of others

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The Hebrew word for father can also mean God; context and occasion determine which sense applies.
rows.anchor: Hebrew is used both to refer to the father and to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: “This” refers to the straight path leading to God; making partners for Him contorts or blocks that path.
rows.anchor: this is the straight path which leads to God

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Jesus clearly called his people to monotheism, but groups among his followers adopted differing beliefs.
rows.anchor: various groups from among his followers adopted different views.

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: After Jesus, only Simon Peter's followers retained monotheism; other sects adopted trinity and atonement, and present Christianity consists of Paul’s innovations and later sectarian interpretations.
rows.anchor: except for the followers of Simon Peter all other sects adopted the beliefs of trinity and atonement

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: Those called unjust are people who wronged themselves through polytheism; they face the punishment of a painful day.
rows.anchor: those people who were unjust to their souls by being inflicted with polytheism

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing section first tells believers and disbelievers their respective fates, then assures the Prophet to disregard mockers, and ends by restating tawḥīd and rejecting intercession as a means of rescue.
rows.anchor: first the believers are informed of their good fate and the disbelievers are informed of their evil fate

rows.speaker: author
rows.claim: The closing reminder says everyone will face the one God, and no one's recommendation can benefit another on that Day.
rows.anchor: each one will face the one and only God, and no recommendation of a person shall avail anyone else.
